title: The Morning Brief: Judge Blocks Visa Freeze; Tariffs Take Effect; Reno Fire Grows
dek: A federal judge struck down the Trump administration's 75-country immigrant visa freeze on immigration law grounds, while U.S.-Canada trade negotiations collapsed and tariffs took effect. Meanwhile, the Hawk Fire near Reno has grown to 15,000 acres, forcing 90,000 evacuations.
author: GoCheckMyNews
key_fact: Three separate policy and crisis developments moved simultaneously Friday into Sunday: a judicial rejection of a signature Trump immigration action; the opening of a major trade war with Canada; and a rapidly escalating natural disaster in Nevada.
bottom_line: Three crises and policy shifts converged over the weekend: a federal court halted a cornerstone Trump immigration policy on statutory grounds; U.S. and Canada entered open trade war with tariffs now in effect and retaliation scheduled for September 8; and the Hawk Fire forced 90,000 evacuations near Reno. A Minneapolis Fed president warned the tariff dispute will extend inflation pressures. Watch for whether the State Department appeals the visa freeze ruling or attempts to reissue denials on different legal grounds, whether U.S.-Canada negotiations resume before September 8, and whether the Hawk Fire's containment improves with weather shifts.
body: A federal judge on Friday struck down one of the Trump administration's most visible immigration policies, finding it violated federal law and exceeded the State Department's authority. U.S. District Judge Jeannette A. Vargas ruled in a 61-page opinion that the January directive freezing immigrant visas for nationals of 75 countries imposed an illegal nationality-based ban. The policy had instructed U.S. embassies and consulates to suspend visa adjudications while the State Department reassessed vetting procedures, citing concerns that applicants from the targeted countries would rely on public benefits. Judge Vargas found the ban violated the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952, which prohibits nationality-based discrimination in immigrant visa issuance, and that it usurped consular officers' statutory authority to assess individual applicants. The ruling vacates all visa denials made solely under the policy and requires reconsideration of those cases. The State Department has not indicated whether it will appeal.

On the trade front, U.S.-Canada negotiations collapsed Friday night before a midnight deadline, triggering immediate enforcement of 50% tariffs on $20 billion in Canadian products including dairy, beverages, cement, and hockey equipment. Canada announced it would match those tariffs dollar for dollar, targeting American steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp, paper, and electronics, with retaliatory tariffs set to take effect September 8. No new talks between the two countries are currently scheduled. Neel Kashkari, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis, warned Sunday that prolonged trade disputes could extend U.S. inflation pressures, saying that once a "new normal" on trade is established, businesses can adjust and inflationary impact will fade.

The Hawk Fire near Reno has grown to more than 15,000 acres since Saturday afternoon, forcing immediate evacuation of 42,000 residents and prompting another 45,000 to prepare to leave. Red flag fire conditions fueled by warm temperatures, low humidity, and strong winds have complicated containment efforts. Approximately 800 emergency responders are battling the blaze, which was confirmed as human-caused, though the investigation remains active. The evacuation zone has reached the edge of the University of Nevada campus. At least six people have been injured. Fire officials say the unpredictable wind patterns remain the chief variable in containment timeline.

In other developments: The Justice Department announced a $400 million settlement with TikTok and ByteDance resolving COPPA litigation, with TikTok paying $300 million immediately and $100 million conditional on court action vacating a prior consent decree. The settlement represents one of the largest COPPA recoveries on record, though the DOJ stated no determination of liability was made and TikTok did not admit wrongdoing. Nancy Kassebaum Baker, the first woman elected to the U.S. Senate without following a spouse into office, died at age 94 of natural causes. She served three terms representing Kansas from 1978 to 1997 and later endorsed Democratic candidates and called for President Trump's impeachment after January 6. A federal agent with Homeland Security Investigations shot 25-year-old Jonah Neal during a mental health crisis in Memphis in May, and the family's attorney says body camera footage shows the shooting was unjustified; the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation's ongoing investigation will determine whether the shooting meets legal standards for use of force. A father of a U.S. Navy sailor deployed aboard USS Abraham Lincoln was detained by Border Patrol in Key West on Saturday and faces deportation; DHS confirmed he entered the country illegally, though he has reportedly lived and worked in the U.S. for roughly 20 years. Sean Grayson, the former sheriff's deputy convicted of second-degree murder in the July 2024 shooting death of Sonya Massey, died in prison on August 23 while six months into his 20-year sentence; he had been battling colon cancer. A landfill collapse in Conakry, Guinea killed at least 30 people and injured 22 others after heavy rain overnight; rescue operations involving military personnel are ongoing. King Harald V of Norway, 89, remains hospitalized with a worsening bacterial bloodstream infection; Crown Prince Haakon is serving as regent. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the U.S. will sever all economic ties with Iran and isolate any nation doing business with Tehran, describing the measures as a new economic offensive; Iran's currency hit a record low in response, and Tehran countered that it would shut down regional oil exports if the conflict continues. Kyle Kirkwood won the Freedom 250 Grand Prix, the first-ever IndyCar race held on downtown Washington D.C. streets, which featured the longest straightaway running down Pennsylvania Avenue between the Capitol and the White House.
